title: Conditional Statements
overview: Programs need to make decisions. Without conditionals, a program just executes every line from top to bottom — no exceptions. Conditionals give your code the ability to think, choose, and respond differently based on what's happening.

blocks.content: Every day you make decisions based on conditions. If it's raining, take an umbrella. If the traffic light is red, stop.
Python's `if` statement works exactly the same way. It checks a condition, and only runs the indented code below it if that condition is `True`.

The structure is simple:

```
if condition:
    do this
```

The colon `:` is required. The indented block (4 spaces or 1 tab) only runs when the condition is True.

blocks.title: Try It — Basic if
blocks.code:
temperature = 38.5

if temperature > 37.5:
    print("You have a fever.")
    print("Please rest and drink water.")

print("Check complete.")
blocks.expectedOutput:
You have a fever.
Please rest and drink water.
Check complete.

blocks.content: Notice that `print("Check complete.")` runs regardless — it's at the same indentation level as `if`, so it's not inside the block.
**Indentation is everything in Python.** Unlike other languages that use `{}` curly braces, Python uses whitespace to define code blocks. Use exactly 4 spaces (or one Tab consistently).

analogy.title: Traffic Light
analogy.description: A traffic light checks: is the light red? If yes → stop. The condition determines what happens. If the light isn't red, you keep driving. The if statement works identically.
bullets: The traffic light checks the current color and takes action.
Red means stop, green means go, yellow means slow down.
Only one action happens at a time — based on what the light shows.
analogy.highlightCard: An if-statement checks a condition and runs the matching block of code.

visualization.title: if condition: block runs
bullets: Python evaluates the condition after 'if' — is it True or False?
If True, the indented code block runs.
If False, Python skips that block entirely.
visualization.highlightCard: if condition: → run this block. That's the core of all decision-making in Python.

code.code:
light = "red"
if light == "red":
    print("Stop!")
print("Light checked.")
highlights: The condition after 'if' must evaluate to True or False.
The colon : at the end marks the start of the code block.
Indented lines (4 spaces) belong to the if-block and run only when True.
code.highlightCard: if-statements let your program choose what to do based on the current situation.

reflection.question: What happens to code indented inside an if block when the condition is False?
reflection.answer: It is completely skipped — Python jumps past the entire indented block.
options: It runs but produces no output

blocks.stage1Transition: Python's if-statement works exactly like a traffic light. Let's see how.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how an if-statement looks in Python code.
blocks.takeaway: A traffic light is a perfect if-statement — it checks the condition (current color) and runs the matching action (stop/go/slow). Python's if works exactly the same way.

blocks.title: Age Verification
blocks.instructions: You're building an age gate for a website. The minimum age is 18. Ask the user for their age. If they are 18 or older, print 'Access granted'. The program should always print 'Verification complete.' at the end.
blocks.starterCode:
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

# Check if age is 18 or above

print("Verification complete.")
blocks.solution:
age = int(input("Enter your age: "))

if age >= 18:
    print("Access granted.")

print("Verification complete.")
blocks.hint: Use if age >= 18: and indent the print statement below it.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Enter your age: Access granted.
Verification complete.

blocks.content: An `if` by itself handles one scenario. But what do you do when you need to handle both the True case AND the False case?
Enter `else`. The `else` block runs only when the `if` condition is `False`.

blocks.title: Try It — if-else

blocks.content: But what if there are more than two possible outcomes? That's where `elif` (else if) comes in. You can chain as many `elif` blocks as you need.

blocks.title: Try It — if-elif-else

blocks.content: Python checks each condition top to bottom. The moment one is True, it runs that block and skips all the rest. So order matters — always put more specific conditions first.

analogy.title: Airport Security Lanes
analogy.description: At an airport: Business class → fast lane. Premium Economy → medium lane. Economy → standard lane. No ticket → denied. Python's elif chain works the same — check conditions in order, use the first match.
bullets: Business class passengers take lane 1, economy take lane 2.
Children under 12 get a special lane, seniors get another.
Each traveler is checked against multiple conditions until one matches.
analogy.highlightCard: elif lets you check multiple conditions in sequence — only one block runs.

visualization.title: elif Chain
bullets: elif stands for 'else if' — it's checked only if the previous if was False.
You can chain as many elif blocks as you need.
Once one condition matches, Python skips all remaining elif and else blocks.
visualization.highlightCard: if → elif → elif → else: Python checks each in order, runs only the first match.

highlights: Python evaluates each condition from top to bottom.
The first True condition's block runs — everything else is skipped.
else at the end is the fallback — it runs if nothing else matched.
code.highlightCard: elif chains let you handle any number of distinct cases cleanly and clearly.

reflection.question: In an if-elif-else chain, when does the else block run?
reflection.answer: When none of the if or elif conditions are True — else is the catch-all fallback.
options: When the if condition is True
When none of the if or elif conditions are True

blocks.stage1Transition: When you have more than two options, Python uses elif. Let's see how it chains.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how an if-elif-else chain looks in Python.
blocks.takeaway: Airport security lanes are like elif chains — each traveler is checked against one condition at a time until a match is found, then directed to the right lane.

If the amount is 0 or less, print 'Invalid amount'. Otherwise print 'Withdrawal successful. Balance: Rs.[remaining]'.

balance = 5000
withdraw = int(input("Enter withdrawal amount: "))

blocks.hint: Check invalid (<=0) first, then insufficient funds, then allow withdrawal.
blocks.expectedOutput: Enter withdrawal amount: Withdrawal successful. Balance: Rs.3500

blocks.content: Sometimes a condition check isn't enough — you need to check another condition inside the first one.
This is called **nesting** — putting an `if` statement inside another `if` statement. Each nested level adds another 4 spaces of indentation.

blocks.title: Try It — Nested if
blocks.expectedOutput:
Age check: Passed
ID check: Passed
Entry allowed.

blocks.content: Notice how the output matches exactly what the conditions dictate. Try changing `has_id = False` and see what happens.

**A word of caution:** Deep nesting (if inside if inside if) makes code hard to read. Often you can rewrite nested conditions using `and` or `or`. For example, `if age >= 18 and has_id:` achieves the same result with less nesting.

analogy.title: Buying a Movie Ticket Online
analogy.description: First check: Is the movie available? If yes → check: Are there seats left? If yes → check: Is the user logged in? Each condition unlocks the next. Nested ifs represent this layered checking process.
bullets: First check: are you logged in? If not, redirect to login.
Then check: is the movie available in your city? If not, show alternatives.
Then check: do you have enough balance? If not, ask to top up.
analogy.highlightCard: Nested if-statements let you make decisions within decisions.

visualization.title: Nested Decision Tree
bullets: A nested if is an if-statement placed inside another if-block.
The inner if only runs when the outer if is already True.
This lets you check a series of conditions in a logical sequence.
visualization.highlightCard: Nest if-statements when the second question only makes sense after the first is answered.

highlights: The outer if runs first — if it's True, the inner if is evaluated next.
Each level of nesting adds 4 more spaces of indentation.
Avoid deeply nested ifs — more than 3 levels often means you need a redesign.
code.highlightCard: Nested if-statements handle multi-step decision trees — check one condition at a time.

reflection.question: When should you prefer 'and' over nested if statements?
reflection.answer: When both conditions must be True at the same level — and keeps the code flatter and easier to read.
options: Never — nested ifs are always better
When both conditions must be True at the same level

blocks.stage1Transition: Python lets you put if-statements inside other if-statements. Let's see how.
blocks.stage2Transition: Here is how nested if-statements look in Python.
blocks.takeaway: Buying a ticket involves nested decisions — log in first, then check availability, then check balance. Nested if-statements in Python work the same way: step by step.

blocks.title: Scholarship Eligibility
blocks.instructions: A scholarship has two levels: If marks >= 90 AND attendance >= 90: print 'Full scholarship'. If marks >= 75 AND attendance >= 75: print 'Partial scholarship'. Otherwise: print 'Not eligible'. Use nested or combined conditions. Test with marks=85, attendance=80.
blocks.hint: Use elif with 'and' to combine both conditions for each scholarship level.

keyTakeaways.text: if checks a condition and runs the indented block only when True.
Indentation (4 spaces) defines what's inside the if block — it's not optional in Python.
else runs when the if condition is False — a two-way choice.
elif adds more conditions between if and else — checked in order, first match wins.
In an if-elif-else chain, once a condition is True, all remaining conditions are skipped.
Nested ifs put one conditional inside another — useful for layered decisions.
Use 'and'/'or' to flatten nested ifs when conditions are at the same decision level.

whatYouLearned: The if statement and how indentation defines code blocks
How to handle two outcomes with if-else
How to handle multiple outcomes with elif chains
How to nest conditionals for layered decision making

quiz.question: What is the role of indentation in a Python if statement?
options: It makes the code look pretty
It defines which code belongs to the if block
It is optional and ignored by Python
quiz.answer: It defines which code belongs to the if block
quiz.explanation: Python uses indentation (whitespace) to define code blocks, unlike other languages that use {}. Any code indented under an if statement is part of that block and only runs when the condition is True.
Python checks if marks >= 75 → False (65 < 75). Then checks elif marks >= 50 → True (65 >= 50). Prints B and stops. The else block is skipped.

quiz.question: In an if-elif-else chain, when does Python stop checking conditions?
options: The moment one condition is True
quiz.answer: The moment one condition is True
quiz.explanation: Python evaluates conditions top to bottom. The instant one is True, it runs that block and skips all remaining elif and else blocks.

quiz.question:
How can you rewrite: if a > 0:
    if b > 0: as a single line?
quiz.explanation: When both inner conditions must be True simultaneously, 'and' combines them into one condition. This produces identical logic with cleaner, flatter code.
The else block runs when no previous condition is True. If x is not > 10 AND not > 5, then x must be <= 5. That's when else executes.
